items.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002
items.q: one of my most recent reissue projects was with Artie Shaw, who is now 92

ctx.x: Well I must admit that I look back on it with a good deal of satisfaction. I’ve been very fortunate because in this business in particular, a lot of the associations that you form, at least initially, are accidental as hell. If someone tells me that I have been helpful to this or that career that’s exactly the thing that I want to hear because I have always looked on the role of the producer in a very specific way. Now one of the hardest things, and I’ve been at it, I’m getting perilously close to my fiftieth…

with doing this. The only real serious variation is that I have — I used to say in recent years — but for a lot of years, a lot of my attention has been focused on reissues and obviously the procedures are a little different there. For the most part that makes it possible to get into cliches like well I spent the whole day in the studio with Louis Armstrong or Duke Ellington or Fats Waller, and he didn’t give me a hard time. But that joke got busted about a year ago because one of my most recent reissue projects…

exactly how I learned to swim. And it was, I also will say that, I said it many years ago with what I have learned I would never entrust as valuable and volatile a commodity as Thelonious to anybody as totally ignorant and inexperienced as I was at the time. But fortunately one of the great advantages of that, well basically it’s a 1950s phenomenon primarily, it happened a little before that, it happened a little after that, but the idea of the jazz fan as self-made jazz record producer actually the art owes a…

items.title: Artie Shaw — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Orrin Keepnews and I picked them out.

ctx.x: So you got Jerry Gray, and he’s picking it up from you.

Yeah, between Jerry and me we got most of the book written, up to a point. Joe Lippman I think played piano in the band. I think he wrote a couple too. In any case, that was how that band started. Again, needless to say, it was anything but a commercial success. I have a great knack for non-commercial. I can do a lot of non-commercial things. This last album, last CD I put out is called Artie Shaw: Personal Best. I chose pieces that no-one has heard in 45, 50 years. Orrin Keepnews and I picked them out. The point…
You got an agent, and you got a contract with Brunswick, and you made those recordings that we know.
